title: Sequence-to-sequence models
text:
CHAPTER 17. LANGUAGE: EMBEDDINGS TO ATTENTION
SECTION 17.2. SEQUENCE-TO-SEQUENCE MODELS

Many language tasks map one sequence to another of a different length: translating a French sentence into English, summarizing a document, transcribing speech, or answering a question. Before 2014, machine translation was dominated by statistical systems built from many separately engineered parts. In 2014, two groups showed that a single neural network, an encoder that reads the input and a decoder that writes the output, could be trained end to end for translation. These sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models, built from the recurrent networks of Section 13.4, set the template that the attention mechanism (Section 17.3) and the transformer (Chapter 18) refined.

1. Before: statistical machine translation

Machine translation is as old as computing; the Georgetown-IBM demonstration of 1954 translated a few dozen carefully chosen Russian sentences with rules. From the late 1980s, IBM researchers (Peter Brown, the Della Pietra brothers, Robert Mercer and colleagues) recast it as probability. To translate a foreign sentence f into English e, choose

    e* = argmax_e P(e | f) = argmax_e P(f | e) P(e)

using Bayes's rule (Section 14.1): P(e) is a language model that rewards fluent English, and P(f | e) is a translation model learned from parallel text (sentences paired with their translations, such as Canadian parliamentary proceedings in English and French). Word alignments were learned with the EM algorithm in the "IBM Models 1-5."

By the 2000s, phrase-based statistical machine translation (SMT), as in the open-source Moses system and the early Google Translate (launched 2006), translated multi-word phrases and combined many features (phrase tables, reordering models, n-gram language models) in a log-linear model tuned for translation quality. These systems worked, but they were complex, made of many components trained separately, and they struggled with long-range reordering and fluency.

2. Measuring translation: BLEU

Progress was measured with BLEU (Kishore Papineni and colleagues, IBM, ACL 2002), which compares a system's output against one or more human reference translations. For n from 1 to 4, compute the modified n-gram precision p_n: the fraction of the candidate's n-grams that appear in a reference (each reference n-gram can be matched only as many times as it occurs). Then

    BLEU = BP * exp( (1/4) sum_(n=1..4) log p_n )

with a brevity penalty BP = 1 if the candidate length c is greater than the reference length r, and exp(1 - r/c) otherwise, to stop systems from scoring well by outputting only a few safe words.

Worked example: p_1..p_4 = 0.6, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3. Their geometric mean is about 0.436. If the candidate has 10 words and the reference 12, BP = exp(1 - 1.2), about 0.819, so BLEU is about 0.357, usually reported as 35.7. BLEU correlates only roughly with human judgments, especially for single sentences, but it made fast, repeatable comparison possible. Scores are only comparable on the same test set and tokenization.

3. The encoder-decoder idea

Nal Kalchbrenner and Phil Blunsom ("Recurrent Continuous Translation Models," EMNLP 2013) proposed encoding a source sentence into a continuous representation (with a convolutional encoder) and generating the translation with a recurrent network. In 2014, two papers made the idea work.

Kyunghyun Cho, Bart van Merriënboer, Caglar Gulcehre, Dzmitry Bahdanau, Fethi Bougares, Holger Schwenk and Yoshua Bengio ("Learning Phrase Representations using RNN Encoder-Decoder for Statistical Machine Translation," arXiv June 2014, EMNLP 2014) proposed the "RNN Encoder-Decoder" and used its scores as an extra feature inside a phrase-based system. The paper also introduced a new, simpler gated recurrent unit, later named the GRU:

    z_t = s(W_z x_t + U_z h_(t-1))                (update gate)
    r_t = s(W_r x_t + U_r h_(t-1))                (reset gate)
    h~_t = tanh(W x_t + U (r_t * h_(t-1)))        (candidate state)
    h_t = (1 - z_t) * h_(t-1) + z_t * h~_t

(* is element-wise multiplication; biases omitted; papers differ on whether z or 1 - z multiplies the old state.) Like the LSTM (Section 13.4), the GRU updates its state partly additively, so gradients can flow across many steps; it has two gates instead of three and no separate cell state.

Ilya Sutskever, Oriol Vinyals and Quoc Le at Google ("Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks," arXiv September 2014, NIPS 2014) translated directly with a pure neural system. The encoder, a deep LSTM, reads the source sentence word by word; its final hidden state is a fixed-size vector v summarizing the sentence. The decoder, another deep LSTM initialized from v, generates the output one token at a time:

    P(y_1, ..., y_T | x_1, ..., x_S) = product_(t=1..T) P(y_t | v, y_1, ..., y_(t-1))

Each step outputs a softmax over the target vocabulary. Generation ends when the model produces a special end-of-sentence token, so output length is learned.

Their LSTMs had four layers with 1,000 cells each. On the WMT'14 English-to-French task, the system achieved BLEU 34.8, compared with 33.3 for a phrase-based SMT baseline. Using the LSTM to rerank the 1,000 best hypotheses of the SMT system gave 36.5, close to the previous best result. A surprising trick helped markedly: reversing the word order of the source sentence (but not the target). This puts the first source words close to the first target words, creating short-term dependencies that make optimization easier.

4. Training and decoding

Training uses maximum likelihood with "teacher forcing": at each step the decoder is fed the correct previous target word (not its own prediction), and the loss is the cross-entropy

    L = - sum_t log P(y_t | v, y_<t)

summed over a corpus of millions of sentence pairs. (WMT'14 English-French used about 12 million sentence pairs in Sutskever and colleagues' experiments.) Gradient clipping (rescaling gradients whose norm exceeds a threshold) controlled exploding gradients.

At test time, the most probable output sequence cannot be found exactly, since the number of sequences grows exponentially. Greedy decoding picks the most likely word at each step, which can make early mistakes it cannot undo. Beam search keeps the B best partial translations (the "beam," with B often between 2 and 12):

    1. Start with one hypothesis: the start token, score 0.
    2. For each hypothesis, consider all next words; the new score is the old score plus log P(word | hypothesis).
    3. Keep only the B highest-scoring of the extended hypotheses.
    4. Move hypotheses that produced the end token to a finished list; stop when B are finished or a length limit is reached.

Small example with B = 2: suppose after step 1 the candidates are "the" (log p = -0.4) and "a" (-1.2). At step 2 the best extensions might be "the cat" (-0.4 - 1.0 = -1.4), "a cat" (-1.2 - 0.3 = -1.5) and "the dog" (-0.4 - 1.5 = -1.9); the beam keeps "the cat" and "a cat". Greedy search would have discarded "a" at step 1, even though "a cat" is almost as good overall. Because sums of log probabilities favor short outputs, scores are usually normalized by length.

5. The bottleneck

The weakness of the basic seq2seq model is that the whole source sentence must be squeezed into one fixed-size vector, whether it has 5 words or 50. Cho and colleagues documented, in a companion 2014 paper ("On the Properties of Neural Machine Translation: Encoder-Decoder Approaches"), that the quality of encoder-decoder translation degrades quickly as sentences get longer. Sutskever and colleagues reported that their deep LSTM did not have much difficulty on long sentences, helped by source reversal and model size, but the fixed vector remained an obvious limitation. The solution, letting the decoder look back at all encoder states, is the attention mechanism of the next section, introduced by Bahdanau, Cho and Bengio in a paper posted on arXiv in September 2014.

Other practical problems:

  - Rare words: vocabularies were limited (tens of thousands of words), so rare words became an "unknown" token. Subword units, such as byte-pair encoding (Section 17.1) and Google's "wordpieces," fixed this.
  - Speed: recurrent networks process tokens one at a time, which limits parallelism on GPUs (Section 15.2), a key motivation for the transformer.
  - Exposure bias: during training the decoder always sees correct previous words; at test time it sees its own, possibly wrong, outputs.

6. Neural machine translation in production

Within about two years, neural machine translation (NMT) with attention surpassed phrase-based systems on most benchmarks. Google's Neural Machine Translation system (GNMT; Yonghui Wu and many colleagues, arXiv September 2016) used deep LSTMs with 8 encoder and 8 decoder layers, attention and residual connections (Section 16.3), wordpieces, low-precision arithmetic for fast inference, and beam search with length normalization and a coverage penalty. In a human side-by-side evaluation on isolated simple sentences, it reduced translation errors by an average of 60 percent compared with Google's phrase-based production system. Google Translate began switching to neural translation in late 2016 (according to Google, for Chinese to English first, then for many more language pairs in November 2016). Other companies, including Microsoft, Facebook and Systran, made similar transitions around the same time, and Google's multilingual NMT work showed a single model could translate between many language pairs, even some ("zero-shot") pairs it had not been trained on directly.

7. Beyond translation

The same encoder-decoder pattern spread quickly:

  - Speech recognition: "Listen, Attend and Spell" (William Chan and colleagues, 2015) mapped audio features to characters; earlier, connectionist temporal classification (CTC; Alex Graves and colleagues, 2006) had trained recurrent networks for unsegmented sequence labeling.
  - Image captioning: "Show and Tell" (Vinyals and colleagues, 2014) encoded an image with a convolutional network and decoded a caption with an LSTM.
  - Conversation, summarization, code generation and parsing were all tried as seq2seq problems; Vinyals and Le's "A Neural Conversational Model" (2015) was an early neural chatbot.

8. Why it mattered

The seq2seq models established ideas that remain central: represent text as sequences of tokens with learned embeddings; condition generation on an input; produce output autoregressively, one token at a time, each conditioned on the previous ones; train end to end with cross-entropy; and decode with sampling or beam search. A modern large language model generates text the same way, with the decoder being a transformer and the "input" being the prompt.

9. Summary

  - Statistical MT (IBM Models, late 1980s-1990s; phrase-based SMT in the 2000s) used Bayes's rule and many separately trained components; BLEU (2002) measured progress.
  - Encoder-decoder models (Kalchbrenner and Blunsom, 2013; Cho and colleagues, 2014, who also introduced the GRU; Sutskever, Vinyals and Le, 2014) translated with neural networks trained end to end.
  - Sutskever and colleagues' deep LSTMs reached BLEU 34.8 on WMT'14 English-French versus 33.3 for phrase-based SMT, helped by reversing source sentences.
  - Training used teacher forcing and cross-entropy; decoding used beam search.
  - The fixed-size vector was a bottleneck, especially for long sentences, motivating attention.
  - GNMT (2016) brought neural translation to production at Google.
